title: Quantum Secure Non-Interactive Reductions
authors: Maxwell Gold, Sarah Hagen, Daniel Alabi, Eric Chitambar
abstract: Efficient models for secure computation often rely on offline preprocessed correlations, which subsequently enable private online computation from minimal assumptions. Within these models, the study of secure non-interactive reductions (SNIR) formalizes when one classical correlation can be non-interactively transformed into another, while guaranteeing information-theoretic simulation-based privacy. In this work, we introduce quantum secure non-interactive reductions (QSNIR), a natural extension of SNIR, in which the source and target resource are each a bipartite quantum state. Specifically, when the target resource is classical, our framework enables us to analyze the problem of disseminating private correlations from entanglement, in addition to classical resources. Our primary technical result is that QSNIR privacy in this context can be computed exactly via a semidefinite program (SDP) pair that quantifies an error operationally rooted in a simulation-based cheating advantage. We prove that QSNIR privacy is lower-bounded by a decision problem related to minimum-error state discrimination (MED), and use both definitions to compute exact one-shot privacy errors for universal two-party computation (2PC) preprocessing correlations.
summary: This work introduces Quantum Secure Non-Interactive Reductions (QSNIR) to analyze the security of transforming quantum correlations. It establishes that the privacy loss can be calculated exactly using Semidefinite Programming (SDP) and proves a relationship between this quantum privacy measure and Minimum-Error State Discrimination (MED). This provides a powerful, assumption-free tool for quantifying information leakage in quantum cryptography.
main_problem: The paper formalizes and analyzes Quantum Secure Non-Interactive Reductions (QSNIR), extending classical secure reductions to cases involving bipartite quantum states as resources.
main_result: QSNIR privacy is shown to be computable exactly via a strongly dual Semidefinite Program (SDP) pair, and this privacy measure is lower-bounded by a decision problem related to Minimum-Error State Discrimination (MED).
method: The analysis uses simulation-based security frameworks, operationalizing privacy via a 'guessing game' solved using Semidefinite Programming (SDP) techniques.
model_or_system: The core model involves bipartite quantum states used as correlations, extending the analysis from purely classical resources to include quantum entanglement.
key_observables: QSNIR privacy error ($\delta_{QSNIR}$), MED privacy error ($\delta_{MED}$), and one-shot leakage for 2PC preprocessing correlations.
important_parameters: The analysis involves parameters defining the quantum states and the security parameters $(\epsilon, \delta_A, \delta_B)$ for the reduction.
main_assumptions: The framework avoids relying on computational assumptions like pseudorandomness or one-way functions, focusing on information-theoretic security.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the QSNIR process for correctness and privacy games; Table 1 reports optimal privacy errors for various 2PC correlations.
paper_structure: The paper develops the QSNIR framework, derives the SDP formulation for privacy, establishes the lower bound via MED, and applies the results to compute exact one-shot errors for specific quantum computation primitives.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum information theory, the rigorous mathematical tools developed (SDP formulations for operational security) are highly relevant to characterizing resource limitations in complex quantum systems.
